answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army general · 12th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff · 65th U.S. Secretary of State
answer.sourceLine: The credit to Powell is uncontested and consistent with everything he taught about dissent — but the line reaches print through Oren Harari’s books about Powell, not through anything Powell is documented to have written or delivered. Wikiquote ↗ files it among quotes of Powell drawn from The Powell Principles (2003), with no page and no occasion; we could not tie the wording to any speech, memo or book of Powell’s own.

source.excerpt: “Every organization,” says Powell, “should tolerate rebels who tell the emperor he has no clothes … and this particular emperor expects to be told when he is naked.”
trail: The best available citation is secondhand. Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence in a block headed “Quotes of Powell from The Powell Principles (2003) by Oren Harari” — a book about Powell, with no page number and no date or setting for the remark.

It is not in the 1996 primer everyone credits. We read Harari’s complete “Quotations from Chairman Powell: A Leadership Primer” at GovLeaders.org ↗, which carries the line “©1996 Oren Harari. Reproduced by GovLeaders.org with the author’s consent.” No emperor, no rebels, anywhere in the eighteen lessons.
Nor is it in the deck that circulates under Powell’s own name. The “A Leadership Primer” PDF hosted by the University of North Georgia ↗ contains none of the key words.

The trail runs to Harari’s 2002 book. McGraw-Hill’s own sample PDF of The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell ↗ confirms the 2002 copyright and the chapter list — including “Promote a Clash of Ideas” — though the emperor sentence is not in the freely posted excerpt.
source.cutTag: Reported speech, not a primary source
source.excerptNote: As given in a digest of Oren Harari’s The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (McGraw-Hill, 2002), reposted to a discussion forum in November 2002 ↗. The ellipsis is in that digest, not ours — which means even the longest circulating version has something cut out of the middle.

source.rightsNote: This is a modern quotation, so it is not public domain. Powell’s own words remain his estate’s, and the only publications that carry this wording — Oren Harari’s The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (McGraw-Hill, 2002) and The Powell Principles (McGraw-Hill Professional Education, 2003) — are firmly in copyright. Quoting the sentence with attribution is ordinary fair use; reproducing Harari’s surrounding text is not.

author.name: Colin Powell
author.kicker: The soldier who wanted to be contradicted
author.heading: Who was Colin Powell?
author.metaLine: 1937–2021 · U.S. Army general · Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, 1989–1993 · 65th U.S. Secretary of State, 2001–2005
author.bio: Colin Luther Powell (1937–2021) rose from a New York City ROTC cadet to become the 12th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and, from 2001 to 2005, the 65th U.S. Secretary of State — the first Black American to hold the office. He spent the back half of his career being quoted as a management guru as much as a soldier, largely because a business professor named Oren Harari spun his blunt aphorisms into two bestselling leadership books. Powell’s recurring theme was that the leader who is never contradicted is the leader most likely to be wrong — a lesson he later said he had learned the hard way, calling his 2003 U.N. speech on Iraqi weapons a blot on his record.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong paperwork
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that this is Powell. What almost everybody gets wrong is where it comes from — and how much of it they are leaving off the end.

items.who: “Quotations from Chairman Powell: A Leadership Primer” (1996)
items.why: This is the document the quote is most often filed under. We read Oren Harari’s complete 1996 text, republished with his consent at GovLeaders.org ↗: all eighteen lessons and all of Harari’s commentary. The words “rebels”, “emperor” and “clothes” do not appear anywhere in it.

items.who: The “A Leadership Primer” slide deck circulated under Powell’s name
items.why: The PowerPoint headed “General Colin Powell, Chairman (Ret), Joint Chiefs of Staff” is the other usual suspect. The copy hosted by the University of North Georgia ↗ runs from “Being responsible sometimes means pissing people off” to “Command is lonely” without ever mentioning an emperor.

items.who: The one-sentence version on every quote card
items.why: The reported remark keeps going. A digest of Harari’s The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell, reposted to a discussion forum in November 2002 ↗, has Powell adding “… and this particular emperor expects to be told when he is naked.” Cutting that clause removes the only part where Powell puts himself on the hook.
The naked-emperor picture is not Powell’s invention. It comes from Andersen’s fairy tale, first published on 7 April 1837 ↗; Powell is applying a fable, not coining a metaphor.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: Colin Powell almost certainly said something very close to this, but it survives only as reported speech in Oren Harari’s books about him — Wikiquote ↗ sources it to The Powell Principles (2003) and can name neither a page nor an occasion.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: Powell built a whole leadership philosophy on the idea that the most dangerous thing in an organization is agreement. His 1996 lessons run the same way throughout: don’t be buffaloed by experts and elites, don’t be afraid to challenge the pros, and — borrowing a line from Xerox’s Barry Rand — if you have a yes-man working for you, one of you is redundant. You can read all eighteen of them, republished with Oren Harari’s consent, at GovLeaders.org ↗.

What makes the emperor line land is the second half almost nobody repeats. In the fullest reported version, Powell doesn’t just recommend tolerating rebels in the abstract — he volunteers himself as the emperor: and this particular emperor expects to be told when he is naked. That turns a piece of generic advice into a standing invitation, which is presumably why it survived the trip from a management book into a million slide decks.
detailsBody: Harari wrote two Powell books for McGraw-Hill: The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (2002) and the shorter The Powell Principles: 24 Lessons from Colin Powell, a Legendary Leader (2003). Both present Powell’s remarks as quotations, and neither is a Powell-authored work — a distinction that gets lost the moment a sentence is lifted onto a quote card.

Powell did publish his own books — the memoir My American Journey (with Joseph E. Persico) and the later It Worked For Me: In Life and Leadership — and Wikiquote cites both with page numbers for other lines. The emperor sentence is not among them.
context.pull: The image is Andersen’s. The management advice is Powell’s. The paper trail is Oren Harari’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Every organization should tolerate rebels who tell the emperor he has no clothes." in a section headed "The Powell Principles (2003)", subtitled "Quotes of Powell from The Powell Principles (2003) by Oren Harari", with no page number or occasion.

The complete text of Oren Harari's 1996 "Quotations from Chairman Powell: A Leadership Primer" (all eighteen lessons, ending at "Command is lonely", with the line "©1996 Oren Harari. Reproduced by GovLeaders.org with the author's consent") does not contain the words rebels, emperor, clothes or naked.

McGraw-Hill's sample PDF of Oren Harari's The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell shows "Copyright © 2002 by The McGraw-Hill Companies", a contents list including Ch. 2 "Promote a Clash of Ideas", and Chapter 1 "Know When to Piss People Off"; the emperor/rebels sentence does not appear in this excerpt.

This page, posted 11/19/2002, reproduces a digest crediting Oren Harari's The Leadership Secrets of Colin Powell (McGraw-Hill) and quotes: "Every organization," says Powell, "should tolerate rebels who tell the emperor he has no clothes ... and this particular emperor expects to be told when he is naked."
The "General Colin Powell, Chairman (Ret), Joint Chiefs of Staff — A Leadership Primer" 18-lesson PDF contains no occurrence of rebels, emperor, clothes or naked.

Colin Luther Powell was born 5 April 1937 and died 18 October 2021; he was the 12th Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff (1989–1993) and the 65th United States Secretary of State (2001–2005), the first Black American to hold that office.
"The Emperor's New Clothes" is a fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, first published in Copenhagen on 7 April 1837; the phrase "the Emperor has no clothes" derives from it.

This page summarises the lessons of "The Powell Principles: 24 Lessons from Colin Powell, a Legendary Leader. Oren Harari. McGraw-Hill Professional Education (c) 2003" and includes the bullet "Tolerate rebels", but does not contain the emperor/no-clothes sentence.
Lib Quotes gives "The Powell Principles (2003)" as the sole source citation for this quote, with no page or occasion.
